hints: Focus on what the gradient of a concentration against time graph tells you about rate.
Notice the graph is a straight line from 0 to 10 minutes, so its gradient is constant even as $N_2O(g)$ is used up.
Consider how a solid catalyst works by providing surface area, and what happens when you provide more surface for the same gas.
walkthrough:
**Read the rate from the graph**

Think of rate as how fast concentration falls. That is the steepness, or gradient, of the curve.

$$\text{rate} = -\frac{\Delta[\text{N}_2\text{O}]}{\Delta t} = -\text{gradient}$$

**Explain the straight line**

A straight line has a constant gradient. So the same amount of $\text{N}_2\text{O}(g)$ disappears each minute, even though its concentration is falling.

This means there is no change in rate from 0 to 10 minutes. This is characteristic of zero order behaviour.

**Think about the gold surface**

The gold foil is a heterogeneous catalyst. The reaction happens when $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ molecules adsorb onto the gold surface.

$$2\text{N}_2\text{O}(g) \rightarrow 2\text{N}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$$

**Predict more catalyst effect**

With only a tiny foil and a large amount of gas, the surface is fully covered and limits the rate. Adding more foil gives more active sites, so more molecules can react at once.

Therefore the rate of decomposition increases.

options.A: Correct. Constant gradient means constant rate, so change is none. More solid catalyst means more surface area and more active sites, so rate increases for the same $N_2O$ sample.
options.B: Half right but half wrong. Rate is indeed unchanged because the graph is linear, but it is a mistake to think more catalyst has no effect. For heterogeneous catalysis, rate depends on available surface area.
options.C: Tempting if you apply the usual rule that rate falls as reactant is used up. Here the straight line proves the gradient is constant, so rate does not decrease. The second column is correct, more surface increases rate, but the first column is wrong.
options.D: Incorrect on both ideas. Students choose this by assuming all reactions slow down as concentration falls and by thinking catalyst amount never matters. This reaction is surface limited, so rate stays constant with time but increases with more gold.
